passages.title: Behind the Bars
passages.passage: Whether a zoo can ever be justified is a question that has divided animal lovers for well over a century. Those who defend zoos point (1)____ the species that would by now have vanished altogether had captive breeding programmes not intervened. Critics, (2)____, argue that no enclosure, however spacious, can make (3)____ for the loss of a territory that may once have stretched across hundreds of kilometres. It is the large mammals, rather than the reptiles or the birds, (4)____ appear to suffer most: elephants pacing the same strip of concrete, or a solitary polar bear swimming in endless circles, are sights (5)____ few visitors forget. Not until the 1970s (6)____ the major zoos begin to redesign their enclosures around the needs of the animals rather than the convenience of the public. Since then, a great (7)____ of money has been spent on naturalistic habitats, and the best institutions now devote a large share of their budgets to conservation in the wild. Even so, the accusation that zoos exist chiefly (8)____ entertainment has never entirely gone away. Were every zoo to close tomorrow, the animals already living in them could hardly be released, having never learnt to hunt or to fear predators. The more honest defenders concede that the real question is not (9)____ zoos are ideal but whether they do more good than harm. On (10)____, they insist, the answer is still yes.

questions.explanation: To point to something is to cite it as evidence for your case. At would mean physically indicating with a finger, and out would need an object placed after it (point out the species).

The sentence contrasts the critics with the defenders in the sentence before, so a contrastive adverb set off by commas is needed: however. But is a conjunction and cannot sit between commas after the subject.
Make up for a loss means to compensate for it. Make for means to head towards or to contribute to, and make out means to discern, so neither fits with for the loss.
This is a cleft sentence, It is the large mammals ... that appear to suffer most, and that is the pronoun that completes it. What cannot introduce the second half of a cleft.
Sights is the object of forget in the relative clause, so a relative pronoun for things is needed: that or which. What would make the clause a noun clause and leave sights without a link.
A sentence opening with Not until inverts subject and auxiliary, and the bare verb begin plus the 1970s time frame call for the past auxiliary did. Had would require begun.
The quantifier for an uncountable noun like money is a great deal of. Number pairs only with plural countable nouns, and amount takes large rather than great in idiomatic use.
Something exists for a purpose: exist chiefly for entertainment. As would identify the zoo with entertainment itself, and of does not follow exist.

The structure not ... but whether demands a parallel clause, and only whether can introduce an alternative question after the question is. If is not used to complete the question is and breaks the parallel with the second whether.

On balance means after weighing the arguments on both sides, which is exactly what the sentence describes. On the whole would carry a similar meaning but needs two words, and on average concerns numbers, not arguments.

passages.title: Making the Picture Stay
passages.passage: Long before anyone managed to fix an image permanently, people knew that light could draw. A darkened room with a pinhole in one wall throws an upside-down picture of the street onto the opposite wall, and artists had used the trick for centuries (1)____ an aid to sketching. What nobody could do was make the picture stay. The breakthrough, when it finally came in the 1820s, owed as (2)____ to chemistry as to optics: a French inventor discovered that a certain kind of bitumen hardened (3)____ exposed to light, so that the unexposed parts could later be washed away. His first successful view, taken from an upstairs window, required an exposure of several hours, (4)____ is why the sun appears to shine on both sides of the courtyard at once. Within a decade the process had been refined to the point (5)____ a portrait could be taken in a few minutes, though sitters still had to be clamped into position (6)____ they blur. Hardly (7)____ the technique been announced in Paris when studios sprang up in every capital in Europe. Painters were divided: some declared that their art was dead, (8)____ others seized on the camera as a tool. What strikes a modern viewer most about those earliest pictures is not their technical crudeness (9)____ their stillness, for the streets appear emptied of everything that moved. It was not until faster plates arrived that photography (10)____ capture the crowd rather than the buildings it walked past.

questions.explanation: To use something as an aid means to use it in that role. For would need a purpose (for sketching), and like would only compare the trick to an aid instead of saying it was one.
The equal comparison as much to X as to Y means X and Y were equally responsible. Many cannot stand alone without a plural noun, and as well would not be followed by a second as to.
A reduced clause when (it was) exposed to light drops the subject and be, leaving the conjunction before the participle. After and by would need a full clause or a gerund (after being exposed).

Only which can refer back to a whole preceding clause (the long exposure) and act as subject of is why. That cannot open a non-defining clause after a comma, and this would need a full stop before it.
The collocation is to the point where (or that) something becomes possible. Which would make point the subject or object of the next clause, which it is not.
Lest means 'for fear that' and is followed by a bare subjunctive, which explains they blur rather than they blurred. Unless reverses the logic, and in case would be two words.

Hardly had + subject + past participle ... when is the inverted past perfect pattern for one event following immediately after another. Was cannot pair with been announced, and did would need a bare verb.
The two groups of painters are set against each other, so a contrastive linker such as while or whereas joins the clauses. However is an adverb and would need a semicolon or a full stop before it.
The pattern not X but Y corrects one idea with another. Rather would need but rather or a preceding comma, and than only works after a comparative such as less.
The cleft It was not until ... that puts the main verb in the past, and ability in the past is expressed by could. Can clashes with the past frame, and began would require to capture.

passages.title: Where the Grass Gives Way
passages.passage: Deserts do not advance across the land like an army; they seep. The process (1)____ which fertile ground turns to dust, known as desertification, rarely begins with a shortage of rain. Far more often it begins with too many animals grazing on too little grass, so that the roots which once held the soil (2)____ place are eaten away before they can recover. Once the surface is bare, wind and the occasional cloudburst finish the job, stripping (3)____ the thin layer of topsoil that took centuries to form. What makes the damage so hard to reverse is (4)____ each stage feeds the next: less vegetation means less moisture returned to the air, which in (5)____ means less rain, which means still less vegetation. Farmers on the margins are seldom (6)____ blame; driven by debt or drought, they have little choice but to push their herds onto land that cannot support them. Governments, (7)____ their part, have tended to answer with grand schemes, such as walls of trees planted across entire continents, whose survival rates have often been dismal. Had the same money been spent on fencing, wells and simple crop rotation, the results (8)____ well have been better. There is, (9)____, reason for cautious optimism. Satellite images show that where villagers have been given secure rights to their land, the green has crept back within a generation. The desert, it turns (10)____, can retreat as quietly as it came.

questions.explanation: A process is the means by which something happens, so the preposition of means goes before the relative pronoun. Of which would express possession, which makes no sense with process here.
To hold something in place is to stop it moving. On place is not English, and into place describes movement towards a position rather than keeping it there.
To strip off (or strip away) a layer is to remove it from a surface. Strip out is used for removing contents from inside something, and strip down means to dismantle.
After a pseudo-cleft (What makes ... is), a full clause must be introduced by that. Because is possible in speech but not in formal writing, and how would change the meaning to manner.
In turn signals one consequence leading to the next in a chain. In return means as a reward or exchange, and in time would mean 'eventually', which loses the sense of sequence.
Someone is to blame for a problem; the infinitive here carries a passive meaning. At and for do not follow are seldom with blame.
For their part means 'as far as they are concerned' and introduces what one party did in contrast to another. In their part is not idiomatic, and by would suggest agency rather than viewpoint.

The inverted conditional Had the same money been spent needs a past modal, and might well have expresses a likely but uncertain outcome. Would does not collocate with well in this sense, and should would sound like an obligation.
The gloomy paragraph is followed by good news, so a concessive adverb between commas is required: nevertheless. Despite is a preposition and needs a noun after it, and although introduces a clause.
It turns out means 'it proves to be the case', an aside inserted between commas. Turns up means to appear unexpectedly, and turns over means to flip, so neither carries the meaning of discovery.

passages.title: The Money on the Table
passages.passage: Economists have long been puzzled by tipping. A customer who leaves money on the table after a meal in a city she will never visit again stands to gain nothing (1)____ doing so, and yet millions of people do exactly that every day. The obvious explanation, that we tip in order to reward good service, does not hold (2)____ under examination, since studies have repeatedly shown only a weak link between the quality of service and the size of the tip. What seems to matter far more is habit, together (3)____ a vague sense of what other people would think of us if we walked out without paying it. From the restaurant's point of view, the custom is convenient (4)____ that it shifts part of the wage bill from the owner to the customer. In some countries, indeed, staff are paid a base rate so low that (5)____ it not for tips they could not live on it at all. Critics argue that this arrangement leaves workers at the mercy (6)____ whoever happens to be sitting at their tables, and there is evidence that tips reflect the customer's mood, and even the server's appearance, quite as much as anything the server actually does. Nor (7)____ the system easy to abolish. Several restaurants that tried replacing tips with higher prices found their customers drifting away, apparently because a menu that looked more expensive put them (8)____ even when the final bill was no larger. It is a curious situation: a practice (9)____ almost nobody defends in theory, yet which almost everybody keeps up in practice. Until customers learn to judge a bill by its total rather than by its parts, tipping is here to (10)____.

questions.explanation: You gain something from (or by) an action, so gain nothing from doing so. Of does not follow gain, and for would express purpose rather than result.
An argument that holds up survives being tested. Hold on means to wait or grip, and hold out means to resist or to last, so neither describes an explanation surviving scrutiny.
Together with adds a second item to the first, like along with. And cannot follow together, and together to is not an English phrase.
In that means 'for the reason that' and explains why the custom is convenient. So that would express purpose, and because cannot be followed directly by that.
Were it not for is the inverted form of if it were not for, an unreal conditional meaning 'without'. Was is not used in this inverted structure, and if would need it were after it.
To be at the mercy of someone is to be entirely in their power. To and from do not complete this fixed phrase.
A sentence beginning with negative Nor inverts subject and verb, and the passage's present-tense discussion calls for is. Does would need a main verb rather than the adjective easy.
To put someone off is to discourage them; the expensive-looking menu discouraged the customers. Put out means to inconvenience or extinguish, and put down means to insult or to set something down.
Practice is the object of defends in the relative clause, so that or which links it. Who is reserved for people, and what cannot follow a noun as a relative pronoun.
The idiom here to stay means permanently established. Remain has the right meaning but is not part of the fixed phrase, and last would need a different structure.

passages.title: When the Bells Learnt to Count
passages.passage: For most of human history, time was something you looked up to see. The sun told you roughly where you were in the day, and the stars did the same at night; for anything finer, people (1)____ to make do with the drip of water through a hole or the slow burning of a marked candle. None of these devices was accurate, and (2)____ did they need to be, since nobody's life depended on the quarter hour. The mechanical clock changed that, though not at (3)____ in the way one might expect. The earliest examples, built for monasteries in the late Middle Ages, had no face and no hands (4)____ all; their only job was to strike a bell so that the monks would know when to pray. It was only later that dials were added, and later (5)____ that the minute hand appeared. What drove the improvement was less curiosity (6)____ commerce: merchants needed to agree on when a market opened, and employers wanted to know how long their workers had actually worked. By the eighteenth century a clock accurate to a few seconds a day (7)____ be bought by anyone with money to spare, and towns began to set their bells by it rather than by the sun. (8)____ earlier generations had fitted their work to the light, their descendants fitted it to the dial. Some historians go so (9)____ as to claim that the clock, not the steam engine, was the true machine of the industrial age. Whether or not that is an exaggeration, it is hard to imagine a factory, a railway or a school timetable without (10)____.

questions.explanation: Had to expresses past necessity and is followed by the bare infinitive make. Must has no past form and cannot be followed by to, and were would need forced or obliged before to.
After a negative statement, nor (or neither) opens an inverted clause: nor did they need to be. Not cannot trigger inversion here, and so is used only after a positive statement.

At first means 'in the early stages', which fits a change that arrived only gradually; not at all in the way one might expect (= 'not in the least') also reads naturally, so both are accepted. At last would mean 'finally', the opposite of what the following sentences describe, and at once means immediately.
At all strengthens a negative: no hands at all. In all means 'in total', and of would need any or none before it.
Later still means 'even later', adding a third step to the sequence begun by only later. Again would suggest repetition, and more cannot follow a comparative adverb this way.
The comparison less X than Y says that Y mattered more than X. But would need not rather than less, and then is a time adverb that has no comparative sense.
The clause states what was possible in the past, so the past ability modal could fits the passive be bought. Can clashes with the eighteenth-century setting, and had would require to be.

The two halves contrast the old habit with the new, so Whereas (or While) introduces the subordinate clause. Although would imply a concession rather than a plain contrast, and Instead cannot introduce a clause.
Go so far as to + verb means to take an argument to an extreme. Much does not combine with go in this idiom, and so long as means 'provided that'.

One stands in for a clock, the singular countable noun the sentence has been discussing, and it can refer to the clock as an invention. Them would need a plural antecedent, and this would point to the historians' claim instead.

passages.title: The Sun That Does Not Rise
passages.passage: Above the Arctic Circle there comes a day each autumn (1)____ the sun rises for the last time, skims the horizon and sets, not to return for weeks or even months. This is the polar night, and it is (2)____ no means as uniform as its name suggests. At its southern edge the darkness is really a long twilight, with the sky glowing blue for several hours around noon; only at the pole itself (3)____ the night become truly complete. Those who live through it describe an odd mixture of dread and delight, (4)____ of which they can quite explain. (5)____ from being a season of hibernation, the winter months are busy ones: schools stay open, fishing boats go out, and the towns hang lights along every street to keep the gloom at (6)____. Even so, doctors record a rise in low mood and broken sleep, (7)____ among newcomers who have yet to learn the value of a strict routine. Locals (8)____ by daylight lamps, vitamin pills and, above all, going outside whatever the weather. By the time the sun returns in late January, the community (9)____ without direct sunlight for nearly two months. (10)____ the hardships, few who have watched that first thin sunrise ever describe it as anything but worth the wait.

questions.q: Blank (1): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: A day is a time expression, so the relative adverb when introduces the clause describing what happens on it. Which would need on before it, and where is for places.

questions.q: Blank (2): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: By no means is the fixed emphatic negative meaning 'not at all'. The other prepositions never combine with no means.

questions.q: Blank (3): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: A fronted restrictive only at phrase forces inversion, and the bare verb become in a present-tense description takes the auxiliary does. Is would need becoming, and did breaks the present tense.

questions.q: Blank (4): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Two feelings were named, so the negative quantifier for two, neither, is required. None is used for three or more, and either needs a negative verb, which can quite explain is not.

questions.q: Blank (5): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Far from being denies one description before offering its opposite. Apart from and aside from mean 'except for', and away cannot precede from being in this sense.

questions.q: Blank (6): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: To keep something at bay is to stop it coming closer. At hand means nearby, at length means in detail or eventually, and at large means free or in general.

questions.q: Blank (7): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Notably singles out the group in which the rise is most marked. Namely would claim that newcomers are the only ones affected, and nearly and lately do not fit before among.

questions.q: Blank (8): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: To swear by something is to trust it completely as a remedy. Insist, rely and depend all take on, not by.

questions.q: Blank (9): choose the phrase that fits.
questions.explanation: By the time + present tense points to a future moment, and the state completed before it takes the future perfect will have gone. Had gone belongs to a past narrative, and would have gone is a conditional.

questions.q: Blank (10): choose the word that fits.
questions.explanation: Whatever the hardships is a concessive phrase meaning 'no matter what the hardships are'. However would need an adjective (however hard), and whichever implies a choice between known items.
